issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
For years, Malo had been a carpenter, a job that demanded precision and a steady hand. That day, he was driving home from a job site, a worn-out tape measure still clipped to his belt, when the flashing lights filled his rearview mirror. The stop was supposed to be routine-a broken taillight-but it escalated in seconds. The officer's voice was sharp, his hand moving to his holster. Malo, a slight, soft-spoken man of Cambodian descent, felt his own body betray him; his hands trembled as he reached for his wallet, and the officer read that tremor as threat. He was slammed onto the hood of his own truck, the metal cold and unforgiving against his cheek, his arm twisted behind his back until a tendon in his shoulder popped. The charge was resisting arrest. It was later dropped, but the damage was done.

In the months that followed, Malo couldn't stop the replay. He would be sanding a piece of oak in his workshop, and the smell of his own sweat would drag him back to that asphalt. He began to blame himself, a quiet, corrosive refrain: If I had just stayed calmer. If I hadn't reached for my license so fast. I made him think I was dangerous. This self-blame was his first, most private strategy-a way to impose order on chaos, to tell himself he could have controlled it. But it only made the world feel more dangerous. He started smoking marijuana heavily after work, telling his wife it helped him sleep, but really it was to blunt the edges of memory, to stop the film from playing.

The world itself had become a series of traps. Every delay-a traffic light that stayed red too long, a customer who was late to pick up a cabinet-sent a spike of cold dread through him. He assumed something bad was happening, that the universe was about to spring another ambush. At the construction site, he felt exposed, his back to the open air, and he started positioning himself in corners, against walls, so he could see every doorway. His boss noticed and joked that he was acting like a paranoid cat. Malo laughed along, but inside, he was certain that safety was an illusion he could only manufacture by watching. He could not relax, even at home. He would sit on the living room sofa, his spine pressed into the corner, scanning the windows, while his wife read on the other end of the couch, growing quieter and quieter.

The connection between this constant threat and his strategies became a tightening loop. When he felt the threat-the prickling at the back of his neck, the certainty that a car slowing down outside was a police cruiser-he would reach for the marijuana, or he would mentally replay the event, blaming himself again. You're weak. You froze. That's why it happened. And that self-blame, in turn, fed the threat. The more he blamed himself, the more he believed the world was a place where a simple mistake could get him hurt, and the more he needed to watch his back. Avoidance of thinking about the event itself became a daily effort; he would change the radio station if a news report mentioned police, but the effort of that avoidance left him exhausted and more vigilant.

A few weeks ago, his wife told him she felt like she was living with a stranger. She asked him to sit down for dinner without scanning the room. He couldn't. What finally brought him to a clinic was not the fear of the police, but the fear of losing his marriage. He is terrified that the only way to feel safe now is to stay in a state of constant watchfulness, and that this vigilance will eventually push everyone away. He hopes, quietly, that someone can show him how to turn it off.
